items.body:
I've been look at the zpages support which went to beta in 1.36 ( [KEP-4828](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-instrumentation/4828-component-flagz/README.md) ) and I wanted to provide some feedback on where I think the current design might cause some user confusion, based on differences in output between the `/configz` and `/flagz` output.

From reading the KEP and some testing I understand that the `/flagz` endpoint returns the values set by command line flags passed to the component *or* default values where no explicit configuration flag has been passed. In contrast to this `/configz` returns the running configuration of the component taking into account flags, default values, and configuration files.

As a result, where components have values set from configuration files as well as command line flags, the responses from `/flagz` and `/configz` will be different. Looking at a standard Kubeadm 1.36 cluster, in that setup it occurs in the kube-proxy and kubelet components, as the others either don't use configuration files (kube-scheduler and kube-controller) or don't have a `/configz` endpoint (kube-apiserver).

As an example in the kubelet there are several significant differences in what's returned by `/flagz` and `/configz`, some of them are :-

- `/flagz` reports that anonymous authentication is enabled for the kubelet, however this is disabled in the kubelets configuration file, so in reality it is not enabled.
- `/flagz` reports that the cgroupDriver is `cgroupfs` (this is the default, there's no explicit flag set by the component) but the configuration file sets `systemd` which is reported by `/configz`
- `/flagz` reports `rotate-certificates` is `false`, but this is enabled in the configuration file `rotateCertificates` setting.
  
This could be particularly tricky for the `kube-apiserver` as there is no `/configz` endpoints, so no obvious path for cluster admins to check the full running configuration. 

Currently in the [zpages documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/zpages/) there is no mention of `/configz` which may lead to cluster administrators being unaware of its presence or unaware of the difference in output between `/flagz` and `/configz`

As the goal of this feature is to support cluster administrators in diagnosing issues with running clusters, it would be great to explain the differences between these two endpoints, and ensure that they're available for all components.

items.title: client-go: rest_client metrics lack resource dimensions, making client-side observability difficult

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: sig/instrumentation
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Instrumentation.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

items.body:
### What happened?

Server-side metrics (e.g. `apiserver_request_duration_seconds`) let you measure latency per verb, resource, group, version, and scope.

However, the client-side metrics exposed by client-go's REST layer use only verb (raw HTTP method) and host as labels. This means:

  - You cannot measure client-side latency per resource. "How long do Pod LIST calls take from the controller's perspective?" is unanswerable.
  - LIST and GET are indistinguishable. The client records the raw HTTP method GET for both. The server distinguishes these as separate verbs.
  - No scope information. You cannot distinguish cluster-scoped from namespace-scoped requests.

Debugging client-side latency is difficult because the metrics lack this information.

We could add resource-aware labels to `rest_client` metrics, similar to what server-side metrics already provide:

1. We could add resource , group, version, and scope labels.
2. We could map HTTP methods to API verbs (GET vs LIST) so verb carries semantic meaning.


Additionally, the recently introduced `A Unified Identity for client-go Components for Enhanced Telemetry` ([xref](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HUNewBqN3lk2DSHJaxKZmmhYgt0SNgp9AqpJTY6cfRM/edit?resourcekey=0-uIvQ3ezUROHa6OKjWZUzcw&tab=t.0#heading=h.qtaj715knfkg))  for client-go components provides a name label that Informers and Reflectors propagate to identify which component initiated a request. This identity could also be passed into rest_client metrics, allowing to correlate API requests back to the specific component that made them.

items.title: No clean way to apply feature-gate-gated metric options

labels.name: sig/instrumentation
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Instrumentation.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

items.body:
**Problem**

Some metric options (like [native histogram options](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0275382260bc0d5279b703d21ec7ad4db35b8d78/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/metrics/internal/nativehistograms.go#L33-L40) supported via `NativeHistograms` feature gate, potentially more in future) need to be applied at metric registration time. Specifically, `initializeMetric()` ([ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/metrics/histogram.go#L96)) reads `NativeHistogramsEnabled()` ([ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/metrics/opts.go#L210-L214)) when creating the underlying prometheus object, so feature gate state must be known before any metric is registered.
The problem here is that the current registration setup provides no clean way to guarantee this ordering. Metrics packages (workqueue, restclient, leaderelection, fifo) have historically registered themselves via `init()` which fires at import time, well before flags are parsed and feature gates are finalized.
______________________________

**What was tried**

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137061 attempted to fix this by removing `init()` from those packages and requiring explicit `Register()` calls from each component's `Run()` function, after the feature gates are parsed. This works for in-tree components in `k/k` but introduces 2 problems:

1. Silent breakages for out-of-tree consumers
Projects outside `k/k` (operators, cloud provider controllers, anything using `client-go` or `controller-runtime`) relied on `init()` auto-registration. With it removed, their `workqueue_*`, `rest_client_*` etc. metrics silently disappear with no error or warning

2. `sync.Once` makes correct ordering impossible in practice
The new `Register()` functions use `sync.Once` to prevent double-registration panics, which creates a "first caller wins" problem. Consider an operator built on `controller-runtime`, to avoid breaking its own users, `controller-runtime` must call `Register()` early. That fires the `sync.Once` before feature gates are parsed. Later when the operator calls `Register()` after parsing the feature gates, the call is a silent no-op, consequently native-histograms never get enabled. There is no way for framework authors to avoid this. If they call `Register()` early they block the feature gate from taking effect, if they dont, some other `init()` in the dependency graph may do it instead.
This means the correctness of metric configuration now depends on non-deterministic `init()` ordering across the full transitive dependency graph.
______________________________

**Potential fixes**

1. defer prom metric object creations till after the feature-gates are parsed by making [`legacyregistry`
`legacyregistry.MustRegister`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/metrics/legacyregistry/registry.go#L37) enqueue metrics into a pending set rather than immediately calling `initializeMetric()`. When `ApplyFeatureGates()` is called, the registry flushes the pending set, firing `initializeMetric()` for every queued metric, now with the correct feature gate state set. POC: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138453
2. Move creation of metrics from init() funcs to constructors of the objects that use the metrics. This came up after discussion with @liggitt, who suggested a more principled alternative to the above solution -"if we really need to defer constructing metrics to be feature-gate informed, I'd rather just delay that directly instead of trying to allow them to still be constructed early, but held, and then really for real constructed later". POC: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138914


Would like to hear any other ideas to fix this issue, since addressing this will establish a clean way to use future feature-gated metric options reliably as well.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery

labels.name: sig/etcd
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Etcd.

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently, Kubernetes exposes separate sets of metrics for etcd3 or from the watch cache. Both implement exactly the same interface and methods, but they have totally different metrics. For example, etcd3 exports metric with `apiserver_storage_list_total`,  while the cacher exposes `apiserver_cache_list_total`.

We propose to unify these aligned metrics by introducing a storage label. This would allow users to aggregate metrics across the entire storage layer or filter by specific backend (etcd or watchcache).

**Proposed label**: `storage="etcd|watchcache"`


For example, apiserver_storage_list_total could be unified with a label:

* apiserver_storage_list_total{storage="etcd"}
* apiserver_storage_list_total{storage="watchcache"}

Caveats and Recommendations
* gRPC Metrics vs. Storage Metrics: While etcd client calls are covered by gRPC-level metrics, these are often "unmergable" with application-level concepts like the watch cache. We recommend maintaining aligned metrics at the k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage layer to allow direct comparison of the same logical operations regardless of the serving layer.

## Next Steps

1. Complete the audit of all metrics in [staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/metrics/metrics.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/metrics/metrics.go) and [staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/metrics/metrics.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/metrics/metrics.go).
2. Agree on a final set of unified metric names and labels.
3. Define a deprecation path for the existing fragmented metrics.

### Why is this needed?

This fragmentation hinders observability by:
* Preventing a unified view of storage operations (e.g. type and percentage of request served from etcd).
* Violating [Prometheus best practices](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/naming/#labels), which recommend using labels to differentiate characteristics of the thing being measured rather than embedding them in the metric name.

/sig api-machinery
/sig instrumentation
/sig etcd
/cc @richabanker

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

I would like to propose addressing several observability gaps in the WatchList feature (introduced in [KEP-3157](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/3157-watch-list)). In Kubernetes 1.35 the controllers transitioned from the standard LIST operation to WatchList for fetching initial object sets, the  feature currently lacks the parity in logging and tracing required for effective production debugging.

**Overview of WatchList:**
WatchList allows controllers to bypass the initial `LIST` request in the List-Watch protocol by initiating a single `WATCH` request that includes the initial set of objects. While this reduces server-side memory spikes and improves scalability, the current streaming nature of the response bypasses existing discrete-step tracing and logging mechanisms.

### **Observability Comparison: LIST vs. WatchList**

| Feature | LIST (Legacy) | WatchList (New) | OSS Gaps to Address |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Initial log** | N/A | Emitted as a standard `WATCH` request. | Missing `audit-ID` field in the starting log entry, making it impossible to correlate with other logs. |
| **Access log** | Reports the `LIST` method with accurate latency. | Reported as `WATCH` after session completion. Latency reflects the entire session. | No specific log entry for the completion of the *initial listing* phase. `apf_init_latency` excludes serialization time. |
| **Trace log** | Detailed logs for each step exceeding 500ms. | No trace logs generated due to streaming processing. | Missing traces that can break down streamed response writing into Network, Compress, and Serialize stages. |
| **Latency metric**| `apiserver_request_duration_seconds` (STABLE). | `apiserver_watch_list_duration_seconds` (ALPHA). | Metric needs to reach **BETA** stability for reliable production use. |


Subtasks:
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136084
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136085
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136086
* Tracing WatchList
  * Add trace logs for WatchList
  * https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136002
  * Add timings into audit logs

### Why is this needed?

With Kubernetes 1.35, controllers will switch to WatchList by default. Without these improvements, performance debugging for large clusters (e.g., clusters with >40,000 nodes) becomes nearly impossible, as we lose the ability to determine if a slow initial sync is caused by serialization, compression, or network bottlenecks.

### **Example Logs for Reference**

#### **LIST Method (Legacy)**
**Access log:**
```text
I0102 09:50:22.075010 1 httplog.go:134] "HTTP" verb="LIST" URI="/api/v1/pods?limit=500&resourceVersion=0" latency="4.508309573s" userAgent="kube-controller-manager/v1.36.0" audit-ID="c736a782-3402-4072-8a25-c17f89598189" resp=200
```

**Trace log:**
```text
Trace[1456271344]: "List" audit-id:c736a782-3402-4072-8a25-c17f89598189,verb:LIST (total time: 4507ms):
Trace[1456271344]: ["cacher.GetList" 4507ms]
Trace[1456271344]: ["SerializeObject" 4502ms]
```

#### **WatchList Method (Current Gaps)**
**Initial log (Missing correlation):**
```text
I0102 09:37:41.848779 1 get.go:263] "Starting watch" path="/api/v1/pods" resourceVersion=""
```

**Access log (Latency reflects total session, not just initial listing):**
```text
I0102 09:39:25.708328 1 httplog.go:134] "HTTP" verb="WATCH" URI="/api/v1/pods?sendInitialEvents=true..." latency="1m43.859s" audit-ID="2f3e2ef1-e9ed-49ed-8963-65ddc0c50244" apf_init_latency="3.985s" resp=200
```

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

I would like to propose an improvement to the Kubernetes tracing system to provide more granular visibility into streamed responses. Specifically, I propose wrapping each io.Writer in a wrapper that measures both the latency and the number of bytes processed at each stage of the response writing process.

This improvement would allow the tracing system to break down the overall latency into distinct categories:

1. Network: Time spent sending data over the network.
2. Compress: Time spent in the compression layer (e.g., gzip).
3. Serialize: Time spent serializing objects into the response format.

Each stage should report the accurate size of the data processed and its individual latency. 

Proof of concept: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136001

**Integration with Tracing:** Initial PoC hardcodes the steps, however we could make the implementation generic and properly integrate streamed/concurrent operation into the tracing framework.

**Performance Consideration:** Adding time.Now() and time.Since() calls to each writer call introduces a negligible overhead of approximately 100ns per call. For a response containing 100,000 objects, the total cost would be roughly 10ms.

/cc @wojtek-t @mborsz @richabanker @p0lyn0mial @jpbetz 
/sig scalability
/sig api-machinery
/sig instrumentation

### Why is this needed?

The current implementation of Kubernetes tracing assumes that all computation is executed in clear, discrete steps. However, with the introduction of KEP-5116 (Streaming Encoding for LIST Responses) and KEP-3157 (WatchList), the existing traces have become ineffective for performance debugging.

Currently, traces for streamed responses:

* Mix compression, encoding, and network latencies into a single reported value.
* Show inaccurate values for object sizes (e.g., reporting only the size of the first chunk instead of the total data).

Without this improvement, it is impossible to determine whether a slow response is caused by network bottlenecks, serialization overhead, or compression delays.

**Before**

Streamed response writing results in traces mixing compressing, encoding and network. As result it only shows combined latency and inaccurate values of sizes. As measured on client side, the size presented in "About to start writing response" writer:*gzip.Writer,size:201240 227ms” is incorrect as it’s not the amount of data compressed, but the size of the first chunk. 

```
Trace[1461829279]: ["SerializeObject" audit-id:e2ed459c-4f3c-47e4-abb3-099e8a4ad38d,method:GET,url:/api/v1/namespaces/0/pods,protocol:HTTP/2.0,mediaType:application/vnd.kubernetes.protobuf,encoder:{"encodeGV":"v1","encoder":"protobuf","name":"versioning"} 9230ms (12:49:16.965)
Trace[1461829279]:  ---"About to start writing response" writer:*gzip.Writer,size:201240 227ms (12:49:17.192)
Trace[1461829279]:  ---"Write call succeeded" size:1006056694 9003ms (12:49:26.196)]
Trace[1461829279]: ---"Writing http response done" count:10000 0ms (12:49:26.196)
Trace[1461829279]: [9.244573577s] [9.244573577s] END
```

**After:**

With improved tracing we see three separate latencies: Network, Compress and Serialize. Each shows individual latency measurement and accurate size of data processed. Here we can see that gzip archives around a 5x compression ratio, which checks out on client side.

```
Trace[2139214577]: ["SerializeObject" audit-id:858bb641-5ba4-44d5-8e6a-d60e6609d4ed,method:GET,url:/api/v1/namespaces/0/pods,protocol:HTTP/2.0,mediaType:application/vnd.kubernetes.protobuf,encoder:{"encodeGV":"v1","encoder":"protobuf","name":"versioning"} 9246ms (13:54:00.023)
Trace[2139214577]:  ---"Network" size:188001850 2796ms
Trace[2139214577]:  ---"Compress" size:1006056312 4966ms
Trace[2139214577]:  ---"Serialize" count:10000 1483ms
Trace[2139214577]:  ---"Write call succeeded" 0ms (13:54:09.270)]
Trace[2139214577]: [9.251880697s] [9.251880697s] END
```
**Bonus WatchList:**
```
I0102 15:08:04.102809       1 trace.go:250] Trace[1455537276]: "SerializeObject" audit-id:bfdf3082-2666-44b7-b8cc-0208147aa063,method:GET,url:/api/v1/namespaces/0/pods,protocol:HTTP/2.0,mediaType:application/vnd.kubernetes.protobuf;stream=watch,encoder:{"encodeGV":"v1","encoder":"raw-protobuf","name":"versioning"} (02-Jan-2026 15:08:00.061) (total time: 4041ms):
Trace[1455537276]: ---"Network" size:1003095731 3031ms
Trace[1455537276]: ---"Serialize" count:10000 986ms
Trace[1455537276]: [4.041542797s] [4.041542797s] END
```

items.body:
**Problem**:
We currently have a significant number of metrics that are stuck at [ALPHA](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/metrics/#list-of-alpha-kubernetes-metrics)  (450 as of v1.34) and [BETA](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/metrics/#list-of-beta-kubernetes-metrics) (23 as of v1.34)  stability levels, as well as deprecated metrics (8 as of v1.34) that have not been removed according to our deprecation timeline. This creates several issues:

1. User uncertainty: Users maybe wary of relying on alpha/beta metrics for production monitoring and alerting, yet many of these metrics have been at these levels for multiple releases
2. Technical debt: Deprecated metrics that linger beyond their expected removal timeline add maintenance burden and potential confusion
3. Lack of accountability: There is no clear ownership or process to ensure metrics progress through their lifecycle

We need some way of ensuring the following preferably by automation

1. Graduation tracking
    1. Metrics at ALPHA for more than N releases should either:
        1. Graduate to BETA (with required testing)
        2. Be deprecated and removed
    2. Metrics at BETA for more than M releases should either:
        1. Graduate to STABLE (with required testing and API review)
        2. Be deprecated

2. Deprecation enforcement
    1. Implement tooling/automation to identify metrics that have exceeded their deprecation timeline
    2. Create a release-blocking mechanism or regular audit process to ensure deprecated metrics are removed on schedule

3. Ownership
    1. Each metric should have a clear owning SIG responsible for its lifecycle
    2. Periodic reviews (e.g., quarterly) to assess metric status

**Questions**

1. What should be the maximum time a metric can remain at ALPHA before requiring action?
2. What should be the maximum time a metric can remain at BETA before requiring action?
3. Should we have exceptions for certain categories of metrics?
4. How do we handle metrics where the owning component/SIG is unclear?

/sig instrumentation

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

klog currently strips file paths to only show the base filename in log output (e.g., http.go). When multiple files in different packages share the same name (e.g., staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/net/http.go and pkg/probe/http/http.go), it creates ambiguity.

We should investigate enhancing klog to provide a less ambiguous way to identify the source file for features like --vmodule.


### Why is this needed?

This ambiguity breaks fine-grained logging control. For example, with two files named http.go, it is impossible to use --vmodule to target only one of them. --vmodule=http.go=5 incorrectly applies verbosity 5 to both files, leading to log spam.

This also confuses external logging platforms that cannot distinguish the source of the logs.

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

**Problem Statement:**

Diagnosing Kubelet issues, such as hangs, deadlocks, and unexpected terminations, can be challenging in Kubernetes clusters. When a Kubelet becomes unresponsive or crashes, it often requires in-depth analysis of logs and system state to determine the root cause. Current methods for increasing debug information often involve manual intervention on the node, such as live flag changes or deploying privileged DaemonSets to alter Kubelet's runtime arguments. These methods are not ideal, especially in production environments, as they can be transient, inconsistent across nodes, and require elevated permissions.

**Proposed Solution:**

We propose enhancing the Kubelet configuration options to include better support for on-demand debugging. This would involve allowing cluster administrators to declaratively configure a node's Kubelet instance with settings to produce more verbose logs and detailed crash diagnostics.

Specifically, we suggest adding support for:

1.  **Kubelet Log Verbosity:** Allow configuring the Kubelet log verbosity level (e.g., `--v=5`) through the standard Kubelet configuration file (e.g., via the `--config` flag) or Node system settings. This would enable more detailed logging of Kubelet operations, health checks, and interactions with the container runtime and other components.

2.  **Go Runtime Traceback Settings:** Expose a mechanism to configure Go runtime environment variables for the Kubelet process, such as `GOTRACEBACK`. Being able to set `GOTRACEBACK=system` or `GOTRACEBACK=crash` can provide more detailed stack traces and coredumps when the Kubelet process encounters a panic or a crash, aiding in post-mortem analysis.



### Why is this needed?

**Benefits:**

*   **Improved Diagnosability:** Natively supporting higher Kubelet verbosity and enhanced crash dumps would provide crucial information for root-causing complex node-level issues.
*   **Simplified Debugging:** Reduces the need for manual on-node modifications or temporary DaemonSets to gather debug information.
*   **Consistent Configuration:** Ensures that debugging settings are consistently applied across nodes in a pool or cluster through standard configuration mechanisms.
*   **Proactive Troubleshooting:** Allows administrators to configure nodes in testing environments or specific node pools with enhanced diagnostics when investigating potential issues.

**Use Cases:**

*   Investigating Kubelet unresponsiveness or crashes.
*   Debugging node-to-apiserver communication problems.
*   Analyzing Kubelet interactions with the container runtime (e.g., containerd, CRI-O).
*   Pinpointing issues related to resource management or pod lifecycle events handled by Kubelet.

**Implementation Considerations:**

These settings could be exposed through the KubeletConfiguration API object, making them configurable via the `--config` file. This approach aligns with the existing mechanisms for Kubelet customization.

By integrating these options, Kubernetes users and operators would have more powerful and standardized tools to diagnose and resolve critical node-level issues.

items.body:
### What happened?

On a machine with very coarse timer granularity, event names are not unique because it only depends on the name of the reference object and the time.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9efb7ee53805225cd70d4b4cd522fc22223dd57b/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/record/event.go#L484-L492
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9efb7ee53805225cd70d4b4cd522fc22223dd57b/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/record/util/util.go#L46-L57

This means if multiple events are created at the same timestamp, they will end up overwriting each other instead.  I have seen, for example, an event that contains the reason from one call to `Event()` and the message from a _different_ call to `Event()` (that had a different reason).

I'm happy to provide a PR based on https://github.com/mook-as/kubernetes/commit/aa22cdb2991f09373f932a3eb351a9a243853c88 if that looks reasonable.

/sig instrumentation

### What would you like to be added?

The `kubelet_runtime_operations_errors_total` metric is only created when the first error occurs. If a kubelet has never encountered a runtime operation error, the metric is absent from the `/metrics` endpoint.

This causes false positive alerts in monitoring systems that track metric absence. Our SLO alerting (using Pyrra) triggers pages when either `kubelet_runtime_operations_total` or `kubelet_runtime_operations_errors_total` is missing:
```
absent(kubelet_runtime_operations_errors_total{job="kubelet"}) == 1
```

The `kubelet_runtime_operations_errors_total` counter should be initialized to 0 at startup, ensuring it's always present in the metrics output even when no errors have occurred.

### Why is this needed?

Prometheus counters should be initialized to 0 to ensure consistent presence.
Missing metrics trigger false alerts in SLO monitoring, especially on stable nodes that rarely encounter errors.

items.body:
### What happened

`Kubelet` currently does not expose some memory usage metrics under `/metrics/resource`, even though memory usage information is already available internally through the CRI stats provider.

This causes inconsistent observability and makes it difficult to monitor actual memory usage across nodes, pods, and containers — especially on Windows.

A customer reported this issue: [#112111](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112111) – *kubelet reports wrong memory usage on Windows*.

In response, SIG Windows decided that the kubelet should report **committed memory** when reporting memory usage on Windows, which is implemented in PR [#132047](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132047).

---

### What you expected to happen

Expose memory usage metrics via kubelet’s `/metrics/resource` endpoint for node, pod, and container levels, so monitoring and observability tools can track actual memory usage consistently across OSes.

---

### Background and Context

- **Linux**: Kubelet retrieves `UsageBytes` directly from the kernel’s cgroup subsystem.  
- **Windows**: Kubelet uses **committed memory** as `UsageBytes` ([PR #132047](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132047)), which aligns memory reporting with the actual memory usage of processes.

The goal is to expose these `UsageBytes` values to `/metrics/resource` for both Windows and Linux.

---

### Proposal

Add the following metrics to the kubelet `/metrics/resource` endpoint:

| Metric | Level | Description |
|--------|--------|-------------|
| `node_memory_usage_bytes` | Node | Total memory usage in bytes (sum of all pods on the node) |
| `pod_memory_usage_bytes` | Pod | Total memory usage in bytes for all containers in the pod |
| `container_memory_usage_bytes` | Container | Memory usage in bytes for the container |

**Platform details:**

- **Linux**: usage comes from cgroup `UsageBytes`.  
- **Windows**: usage comes from committed memory (`CommitMemoryBytes`).

---

### Example Output

```
# HELP node_memory_usage_bytes [ALPHA] Usage memory of the node in bytes.
# TYPE node_memory_usage_bytes gauge
node_memory_usage_bytes 2000 1624396278302
# HELP container_memory_usage_bytes [ALPHA] usage memory of the container in bytes.
# TYPE container_memory_usage_bytes gauge
container_memory_usage_bytes{container="container_a",namespace="namespace_a",pod="pod_a"} 2000 1624396278302
container_memory_usage_bytes{container="container_a",namespace="namespace_b",pod="pod_b"} 2000 1624396278302
```
---

### Motivation

- Fix inaccurate or missing memory usage reporting on Windows ([#112111](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112111)).  
- Provide consistent memory usage metrics for monitoring on both Linux and Windows.  
- Enable observability at node, pod, and container levels.  
- Achieve parity between Windows and Linux kubelet metrics.

---

### Impact

- **Metrics/resource endpoint**: adds three new usage metrics for all OSes.  
- **Backward compatibility**: no changes to existing metrics or APIs.

---

### Open Questions

- Is exposing `*_memory_usage_bytes` metrics on both Linux and Windows acceptable?  
- Should the metric naming remain as `*_memory_usage_bytes`, or align differently with other memory metrics?  
- Should this change be behind a feature gate, or merged directly?

This proposal includes two related changes to improve egress traffic visibility from core Kubernetes components and to refine logging controls:

Add Verbose Logging to staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/net/http.go: Introduce new klog V-level logs to provide visibility into outbound HTTP requests and how they are handled by proxy settings.

A V(5) log will be added to record requests that are proxied (i.e., not matching the NO_PROXY environment variable). This helps identify traffic that would be blocked in a restricted environment.

A V(6) log will be added to record requests that are not proxied (i.e., explicitly allowed via NO_PROXY). This helps verify that allowlist rules are functioning as expected.

Rename pkg/probe/http/http.go to pkg/probe/http/http_prober.go: Rename this file to prevent a logging conflict with the file mentioned above, which is the actual target for our enhanced logging.

### Why is this needed?

Downstream distributions of Kubernetes, such as GKE, are implementing security features to strictly control and block all egress traffic originating from the kube-apiserver. A core part of this mechanism involves using HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY environment variables to route traffic through a controlled gateway or a "blackhole" proxy, while using a NO_PROXY variable to allowlist essential cluster endpoints.

To safely roll out such a feature, it is critical to have a data-driven way to discover and audit all outbound requests made by the kube-apiserver and other components. This allows operators to build a comprehensive NO_PROXY allowlist and ensure no critical functions are broken. The proposed verbose logging in net/http.go provides this essential visibility.

The second change—renaming pkg/probe/http/http.go—is necessary to avoid unintended log spam. The klog output strips the full file path, so both staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/net/http.go (our target) and pkg/probe/http/http.go (an unrelated file) show up in logs simply as http.go.

As a result, setting --vmodule=http*=5 to enable our new logs also enables verbose logging in the probe helpers, flooding the logs with messages from liveness and readiness probes. This makes it extremely difficult to isolate the critical egress traffic data needed for validation. Renaming the probe helper file to http_prober.go cleanly resolves this name collision and allows for precise, targeted logging for this important security use case.

### What would you like to be added?

The scheduler should generate an OTEL trace for a single scheduling attempt of a pod.

### Why is this needed?

We've observed slow scheduling attempts for pods which can be cumbersome to investigate with multiple scheduling plugins enabled. It would be very useful to have a trace for a single pod scheduling attempt. The trace context could also be propagated to custom scheduler plugins. 

One benefit of this over the existing log-based `utiltrace` is downstream clients that have already instrumented OTEL tracing (ie. http clients) could now be visualised in the context of a scheduling attempt.

The existing `utiltrace` is quite useful, but is k8s specific. Given [other k8s components](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/system-traces/#component-traces) standardising around OTEL traces, feels appropriate for the scheduler to as well.

items.body:
The current implication of [DeprecatedVersion](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.33/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/metrics/opts.go#L60) for a metric(like [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.33/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/metrics/metrics.go#L83)) is confusing.

According to the [Metrics Deprecation Rules](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/deprecation-policy/#deprecating-a-metric) we want to first announce the deprecation of a metric and then stop serving them after a recommended period of time (for stable metrics, this is noted as: STABLE: 3 releases or 9 months (whichever is longer)). So seems like the metric should continue to function properly after its marked as deprecated.

But we recently caught an [issue](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133405) that was 1.34.0 release blocking, where a STABLE metric marked as deprecated for 1.34.0 caused a panic in apiserver startup, because it was actually being removed in 1.34.0. It seems like the DeprecatedVersion here is actually behaving like RemovedVersion, where we stop serving the metric in K8s version greater than the specified value.


Questions:

1. What does the DeprecatedVersion mean here? Is it supposed to be the version where we mark the metric for deprecation but continue serving it for stated timeline in the guidelines, after which we actually remove the support for it? Or, is it the version post which we will stop serving the metric?

3. Based on the above, are we sure about the behaviour/support for `apiserver_storage_objects` metric (which was what caused [this](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133405) issue) that will be reflected in 1.34.0 ?

items.title: Expose timestamp for metric based on cached value

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/instrumentation
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Instrumentation.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Prometheus protocol expects that metric values are fetched ad-hoc. It fetches the metric from endpoint and assign timestamp based on scape time. However there are cases where calculating metric is very expensive.

Apiserver has multiple such metrics, where getting metric value would require processing large amount of data and even fetching data from etcd. In such cases the metric is calculated periodically and cached for prometheus to scape. This however means that metric values are stale. Example metrics:
* [apiserver_storage_objects](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b1b15a57e68338099daa4b934b6235db4c429a66/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/metrics/metrics.go#L70-L77)
* [storage_db_total_size_in_bytes](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b1b15a57e68338099daa4b934b6235db4c429a66/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/metrics/metrics.go#L78-L87)
...


Even if we agree that such metrics don't need to be fresh, serving metric based on cached values creates a problem, how to represent cache being stale. What if the periodic calculation has not succeeded for 10 minutes? We cannot just expose the same value. Example solution used by [apiserver_storage_objects](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b1b15a57e68338099daa4b934b6235db4c429a66/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/metrics/metrics.go#L70-L77) is to set metric value to -1. This however causes issues with aggregation. Other solution would be to remove the metric, however this would result in metric totally disappearing causing user confusion.

Proper solution would be to acknowledge that metric is not calculated ad-hoc, but was calculated some time ago. That way if the cache is stale, old metric value will be still exposed, but will stop calculations and breaking aggregations. This should be achievable by using https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus#NewMetricWithTimestamp

/sig instrumentation
/cc @richabanker @jpbetz 

### Why is this needed?

Fixes freshness and aggregation of metric calculated based on cache.

items.body:
In the original implementation of [statusz](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/125577#discussion_r1821356236), we removed the hard-coded paths (/healthz, /livez, /readyz)  which would show up under "Useful Links" since not all paths were relevant for all components.

A better way to add this section is to tailor that section separately for each component, so it shows all paths actually exposed by a particular component (which may not necessarily be same across all control plane components)
